Lesson 9: Tragedy

Tragedy

The Meaning of "Tragedy"

Before you read the play, it might be useful to consider the nature of tragedy.

When you hear the word "tragedy" what do you think of? If you are like most people, you think of sad, unhappy events - misfortunes that ruin people's lives. But as you'll recall, in the field of drama a distinction has to be drawn between tragic events and occurrences that are simply pathetic. If something dreadful happens to someone because of forces outside of that person's control (for example, if another driver smashes into his or her car), it can be said to be pathetic but not technically tragic. A tragic event, by contrast, depends on a relationship between people's behaviour and the events that happen to them. Thus, tragic "heroes" must in some way be responsible for what happens to them; their downfalls must somehow result from their actions and choices, at least in part.

Of course, a tragedy in this technical sense isn't entirely divorced from the way people ordinarily use the word. Plays that involve unfortunate events befalling their protagonists - events that destroy their lives and usually result in their deaths - can in a loose sense be called tragedies. Great tragedies, however, don't depress their audiences the way simply pathetic occurrences likely would. Although they involve sadness and suffering, real tragedies can serve to uplift those who witness them and leave viewers feeling emotionally cleansed and refreshed.

This notion of what a tragedy is goes back to the Greek philosopher, Aristotle, who lived from 384 to 322 BCE.

In his work the Poetics, Aristotle argued that tragedy is a type of drama that deals with events arousing pity and fear, but at the same time bringing a catharsis of these emotions. In other words, the audience watching a tragedy should experience an emotional release as well as a feeling of spiritual uplifting.

According to Aristotle, the protagonists of tragedies should be people of exceptional ability, and usually of noble rank within society (in Aristotle's day, rank was arguably more socially important than it is today). However, more importantly, tragic heroes should possess nobility of soul. Tragic heroes should be people capable of much, but because of some flaw in themselves, their lives are brought from the heights down to the depths, from happiness down to misery.

The Tragic Hero

The term tragic hero implies two separate concepts: tragedy and heroism. Tragic heroes must be people of noble stature. They have a greatness about them. They aren't ordinary people but individuals of outstanding qualities. In Greek and in Shakespearean tragedy, they are usually princes or kings; however, they are great not simply because of their positions but because of their possession of extraordinary abilities - qualities of passion or aspiration or nobility of mind.

Even though tragic heroes are great, they aren't perfect. Some critics believe that combined with their strength, there is also a weakness. Aristotle said that the falls of tragic heroes are usually caused primarily by a form of pride called hubris. There is no English word that accurately translates this Greek word. Think of it as the attitude people have when they act as if they can do anything and not suffer the consequences. It is a form of pride, but it's also a feeling of power, will, and self-confidence. Ordinarily, this sense of confidence is a good thing; however, when it is combined with hamartia, or error of judgment, it can, and often does, end in tragedy.

This hubris, combined with error in judgment, emphasizes that a tragic hero isn't perfect. A tragic hero has a character flaw - the so-called tragic flaw.

With all of their great qualities, tragic heroes are afflicted with some fault of character such as inordinate ambition, a quickness to anger, a tendency to jealousy, or the inability to act simply because they think too much. This flaw in their characters leads to their downfalls.

Nevertheless, the misfortunes of tragic heroes aren't wholly deserved. The audience doesn't come away from a real tragedy with the feeling that the hero "got what he had coming to him" but rather with the sense of a waste of human potential, for what most impresses us about tragic heroes isn't their weakness but their strengths. They are, in a sense, "larger than life", and they reveal to us the dimensions of human possibility. They are people who are for the most part admirable, and their falls, therefore, fill us with regret and fear.

Yet such tragic falls aren't pure loss. Though they may result in the protagonist's deaths, they involve, before the deaths, some increase in awareness, some discovery of truth or gain in self-knowledge and wisdom. This increase in wisdom usually involves some sort of reconciliation with the universe or with the protagonist's situation. Tragic heroes exit not cursing their fate but accepting it and acknowledging that to some degree it is just.

Indeed, many people, after sitting through an intense production of a tragedy such as Hamlet or Othello, leave the theatre feeling exhilarated and somehow purified; along with this there goes a gain in wisdom - the sense that through watching the destruction of a noble soul, increased self-awareness and understanding have been gained. There is, of course, the sadness and regret you might expect over the waste of human potential, but through this, a greater understanding of the human condition should have been achieved.

Lesson 10: The Principal Characters

Approaching Othello: The Principal Characters

Read over the following list of characters sketches to get an idea of the connections between them.

Roderigo - a Venetian gentleman; rejected suitor to Desdemona

Iago - newly appointed ensign to Othello

Brabantio - Venetian Senator; father to Desdemona

Othello - the Moorish General - Moor of Venice, husband to Desdemona

Cassio - newly appointed lieutenant to Othello

Duke of Venice - official who appoints Othello in charge of Cyprian mission

Desdemona - wife to Othello; daughter to Brabantio

Montano - retiring governor of Cyprus; predecessor to Othello in Cyprian government

Emilia - wife to Iago; attendant to Desdemona

Clown - servant to Othello

Bianca - a courtesan; mistress to Cassio

Gratiano - Venetian nobleman; brother to Brabantio

Lodovico - Venetian nobleman; kinsman to Brabantio

Senators - officials who discuss Cyprian mission

Messengers - deliver announcements during the play

Two Gentlemen - converse with the governor

Third Gentleman - brings news of the Turkish fleet

Herald - Othello's herald who reads a proclamation

Sailor - brings message about Turkish fleet

Officers - unnamed characters throughout the play who serve in the military

Attendants - unnamed characters throughout the play whose purpose is to serve the other characters

Pronoun Power

Choose the correct Elizabethan form of you by thinking about subject, object, and possession.

I give this sword to .

Object of the sentence: the person receiving the action.

art my most loyal friend.

Subject of the sentence: the one doing the action.

Do not forget honor.

Possessive adjective: it comes right before the noun.

The victory is completely .

Possessive pronoun: it stands on its own.

Dost bite thy thumb at us, sir?

Subject form: the person doing the action of biting.

Dost thou bite thumb at us, sir?

Possessive adjective: it describes whose thumb it is.

I pray , hear my counsel.

Object form: the person being addressed or appealed to.

Form and Structure

Controlled organization, paragraphs, transitions, and unity.

Accurate grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling, and sentence control.

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Personal Response to Text Guide

Use this six-stage studio to connect a meaningful play idea to precise evidence and your own knowledge or experience in a purposeful prose form.

I can...

  • I can explore an idea, feeling, or impression prompted by the play.
  • I can use precise play evidence and relevant knowledge or experience.
  • I can choose a prose form and perspective that suit my purpose.
  • I can revise for development, voice, clarity, and correctness.

Personal response focus

A personal response explores an idea or impression from the play, supports it with precise evidence, and connects it to knowledge or experience in a purposeful prose form.

Idea or Impression

A focused response to the prompt that is worth exploring.

Play Support

Precise act, scene, line, stage direction, action, or dramatic choice.

Knowledge or Experience

A relevant connection that deepens the meaning of the response.

Prose Form

A purposeful structure suited to the idea, audience, and effect.

Perspective and Voice

A personal, critical, creative, or blended approach.

Your writing path

Complete the six lessons in order. The final Preview combines the work saved in the active track exactly as entered.

  1. Prompt and Initial Impression
  2. Play Evidence
  3. Knowledge and Experience
  4. Prose Form and Perspective
  5. Shape the Response
  6. Draft and Revise
  7. Personal Response Preview

Prompt and Initial Impression

Understand the prompt and decide what idea, feeling, or impression you want to explore.

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Othello

Prompt and Initial Impression
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can identify what the prompt asks me to explore.
  • I can name a genuine reaction to the play.
  • I can turn that reaction into a focused idea.

Lesson

Separate the prompt from your first response, then turn that reaction into a focused controlling idea.

Model move

Begin with a genuine idea, feeling, question, or image from Othello, then shape that reaction into a focused direction.

Example

Identify one moment from Othello that stayed with you and explain the human question it raises for you.

Writing tip

Choose an impression that you can explore, not merely a like-or-dislike reaction.

How to apply it

  1. Restate the prompt in your own words.
  2. Name the moment or impression that stays with you.
  3. Explain why it matters to you.
  4. Shape the reaction into one controlling idea.

Play Evidence

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Play Evidence
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can identify a precise play moment.
  • I can explain the playwright's choice.
  • I can connect the evidence to my controlling idea.

Lesson

Use an act, scene, line, stage direction, action, or dramatic choice as meaningful support.

Model move

Use one precise moment from Othello, identify the playwright's choice, and explain how it deepens your controlling idea.

Example

Record a quotation, image, action, scene, or exact detail and explain the effect it creates rather than leaving the evidence to speak for itself.

Writing tip

Include a locator and only the context your reader needs.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the strongest moment for your idea.
  2. Record the evidence and its locator.
  3. Name the playwright's deliberate choice.
  4. Explain how the moment develops your response.

Knowledge and Experience

Connect the play's idea to relevant personal knowledge, observation, or experience.

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Othello

Knowledge and Experience
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can choose a relevant connection.
  • I can explain why the connection matters.
  • I can link the connection back to the play and prompt.

Lesson

Choose a connection that deepens the response rather than replacing discussion of the play.

Model move

Connect Othello to relevant knowledge, observation, or experience, then return to the work with a deeper understanding.

Example

Use a specific memory, observation, or piece of learning that genuinely changes how you understand the selected moment.

Writing tip

The connection supports the response; it should not replace discussion of the work.

How to apply it

  1. Choose one relevant connection.
  2. Describe it precisely enough to be understood.
  3. Explain the insight it creates.
  4. Link that insight back to the work and prompt.

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Prose Form and Perspective

Choose the form and perspective that best communicate your idea.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Othello

Prose Form and Perspective
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can choose a prose form that suits my purpose.
  • I can choose a clear perspective and voice.
  • I can identify the audience and effect I want.

Lesson

The response may be personal, critical, creative, or blended, but every choice must remain grounded in the play and prompt.

Model move

Choose the prose form, perspective, audience, and voice that make the controlling idea most effective.

Example

A letter, editorial, monologue, short essay, or blended response should sound and move differently because each form creates a different relationship with the reader.

Writing tip

Let purpose determine the form. Do not choose a creative form unless its structure strengthens the idea.

How to apply it

  1. Clarify your audience and purpose.
  2. Choose a prose form suited to that purpose.
  3. Select a perspective and voice.
  4. Plan how the form will shape the opening, development, and ending.

Shape the Response

Plan an opening, development, and ending that suit your chosen prose form.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Othello

Shape the Response
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can open in a way that suits my form and voice.
  • I can develop the play and personal connection coherently.
  • I can end with a meaningful final insight.

Lesson

Arrange the play evidence and personal connection so the response develops rather than becoming a list of separate ideas.

Model move

Arrange the Othello evidence and personal connection so each part develops the same controlling idea.

Example

Plan an opening that establishes voice, a development that connects evidence and experience, and an ending that leaves a meaningful final insight.

Writing tip

Build progression. Avoid placing text evidence and personal experience in disconnected blocks.

How to apply it

  1. Draft an opening suited to the chosen form.
  2. Order the work evidence, analysis, and connection.
  3. Plan transitions that show development.
  4. Draft an ending that completes the response.

Draft and Revise

Write the complete response and revise it for support, form, voice, and correctness.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-1 | Personal Response Writing

Othello

Draft and Revise
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can sustain my controlling idea through the full response.
  • I can integrate play support and personal knowledge purposefully.
  • I can revise for form, voice, clarity, and correctness.

Lesson

Use the plan as a foundation, then make the final response sound intentional and complete in its chosen form.

Model move

Use the plan as a foundation, draft the complete response, then revise for meaning, form, voice, clarity, and correctness.

Example

Read the complete draft once for the controlling idea, once for support and development, and once for sentence-level correctness.

Writing tip

Revise the larger meaning and structure before proofreading individual errors.

How to apply it

  1. Draft the complete response in the chosen form.
  2. Check that every section develops the controlling idea.
  3. Strengthen evidence, explanation, and connection.
  4. Revise voice, sentences, grammar, punctuation, and spelling.
